power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: To evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM).
Cross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging.
1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic.
Glycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c.
Center-of-mass mean lifetime (τCMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans.
Group differences in central-window τCMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on τCMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age.
Macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV).

Group-averaged τCMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age.

For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 ± 0.04), compared with 0.51 ± 0.03 for an age-only classifier.
ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance.
Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 ± 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 ± 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 ± 0.04 (XGBoost).
All three FLIO models exceeded the ageonly classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance.

FLIO-derived τCMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models.
These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a major global health burden and a leading cause of vision loss worldwide.
Early detection and monitoring of metabolic dysregulation are essential for preventing complications, including diabetic retinopathy (DR).
Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), which reflects average blood glucose levels over the preceding two to three months, is widely used to assess long-term glycemic control in routine clinical care.
However, HbA1c measurement requires invasive blood testing and may not capture tissue-specific metabolic changes.
The retina is uniquely positioned to serve as a window into assessing metabolic health through noninvasive retinal imaging techniques.

Prior studies have explored the use of fundus photography and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) for diabetes and DR classification, demonstrating that retinal images contain predictive signals for systemic disease states, but these modalities provide limited insight into time-resolved biochemical processes.
However, OCT and fundus autofluorescence (FAF) primarily capture static structural or intensity-based information and do not directly measure dynamic fluorescence properties.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) is a non-invasive imaging technique that measures the decay time of endogenous retinal fluorophores following laser excitation. 1, 2 It utilizes a 473 nm laser for the excitation of fluorophores, and fluorescence emission is detected by a time-correlated single photon counting system in two distinct spectral channels: the short spectral channel (SSC: 498-560 nm) and the long spectral channel (LSC: 560-720 nm). 3 The photons from the fluorophores, including flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD), macular pigment, collagen, elastin, and advanced glycation end products (AGE), are considered to be predominantly detected in the SSC; and the fluorescence from A2E and lipofuscin, in the LSC. 4 In contrast to FAF, FLIO quantifies both fluorescence intensity and the duration of the excited state (fluorescence lifetime), providing information about the biochemical metabolic processes within retinal tissue.

text.text: Schweitzer et al. pioneered the application of time-resolved autofluorescence to the human fundus and demonstrated that fluorescence lifetime parameters reflect the biochemical and metabolic processes of retinal tissue. 1 Subsequently, they showed that patients with T2DM, even in the absence of clinically apparent DR, exhibit prolonged fundus autofluorescence lifetimes, with specific lifetime components correlating with HbA1c levels. 5 Schmidt et al. extended these findings to patients with non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), showing increased lifetimes across all Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) grid regions relative to healthy controls. 6 Collectively, these studies suggest that FLIO captures a metabolic signature of patients with T2DM that precedes structural retinal damage, motivating the investigation of FLIO as a pre-symptomatic marker of systemic glycemic state.

text.text: Despite the promising prior studies on FLIO and metabolic monitoring, most prior FLIO analyses apply multi-exponential curve fitting to model fluorescence decay signals, typically decomposing the signal into short and long lifetime components and deriving summary parameters such as amplitude-weighted mean lifetimes.

While biologically interpretable, these approaches depend on predefined model assumptions, are sensitive to initialization and noise, and may not fully capture the complex, high-dimensional structure of fluorescence decay data.

In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI), especially deep learning models, applied to retinal imaging modalities such as fundus photography and OCT have demonstrated strong performance in predicting systemic biomarkers and disease states directly from images, often without explicit feature engineering. [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] Deep learning has been shown to estimate mean lifetime parameters comparable to those obtained with multiexponential fitting in fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM), the broader imaging modality on which FLIO is based. 12 Despite these advances, deep learning approaches have not yet been explored for FLIO data, except one study where several state-of-the-art AI models were developed to classify smokers vs non-smokers based on FLIO signals, a goal substantially different from ours on T2DM classification. 13 In this study, we investigate whether AI can detect metabolic signatures from FLIO to classify diabetes status.

To reduce noise in photon measurements, spatial binning was applied prior to lifetime estimation.
Specifically, for each temporal frame, pixel intensities were averaged within a 3 × 3 neighborhood.

Spatial maps were generated using the center-ofmass method (CMM).

text.text: We developed and evaluated convolutional neural network (CNN), ResNet-18, and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models to classify glycemic status from spatial τCMM maps.
All models made one prediction per participant.

The primary task was three-class classification of normal, prediabetic, and diabetic status; we also evaluated two binary classification tasks: normal versus impaired glycemia and normal versus diabetes.

Because retinal anatomy is approximately mirror-symmetric between fellow eyes, right-eye maps were horizontally flipped to the left-eye (OS) orientation before encoding (laterality canonicalization), so that both eyes share a common anatomical frame; canonicalization was applied during training and inference for all models.
CNN inputs and architecture.

For each eye, the SSC and LSC τCMM maps (256 × 256 pixels), each standardized to zero mean and unit variance over its valid pixels, were stacked as a two-channel input image and processed by a shared CNN encoder.

The encoder consisted of four convolutional blocks with 3 × 3 kernels; each block included batch normalization and rectified linear unit activation, the first three were followed by max pooling, and the number of feature channels increased from 32 to 256 across successive blocks.
The final convolutional features were aggregated by adaptive average pooling into a 256-dimensional eye embedding.

The embeddings of a participant's available eyes (one or two) were mean-pooled into a participant-level embedding, which was then passed to a fully connected classification head with dropout regularization.
The output layer generated class logits, which were converted to class probabilities using a softmax function.
Variations in CNN depth, channel width, and regularization were evaluated during model development; detailed configurations are provided in the Supplementary Materials Section A.
ResNet-18 inputs and architecture.

ResNet-18 was evaluated as a second image-based model using the same two-channel τCMM input, laterality canonicalization, and participant-level mean pooling as the CNN, with the first convolutional layer adapted to two input channels.
ResNet-18 uses residual blocks with identity skip connections to facilitate optimization of deeper networks.
ResNet-18 was trained from random initialization and class-weighted cross-entropy loss.
Additional architectural and implementation details are provided in the Supplementary Materials Section A.
XGBoost inputs and architecture.

Unlike the image-based models, XGBoost was trained using summary features extracted from the laterality-canonicalized τCMM maps: the mean τCMM within the superior, nasal, inferior, and temporal sectors of the inner ring of the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) grid for the SSC and of the outer ring for the LSC, following prior work. 13 Sector means were averaged over a participant's eyes and supplemented with derived features (per-sector SSC -LSC differences, SSC/LSC ratios, and SSC-LSC means; the mean, standard deviation, minimum, maximum, and range across the eight sector means; and four within-channel products of sector means), yielding 29 features.

text.text: Hyperparameters-including tree depth, learning rate, subsampling rate, and regularization parameters-were selected within the inner cross-validation procedure (Supplementary Materials Section A).
To assess whether FLIO adds information beyond age, each model was also trained with age as an additional input.

For the CNN and ResNet-18, age, standardized to zero mean and unit variance, was concatenated to the pooled participant embedding before the classification head; for XGBoost, age was added to the feature set.
An XGBoost classifier trained on age alone served as the ageonly baseline.
Classification tasks.
The three-class task classified participants as having normal glycemia, prediabetes, or diabetes.
Because prediabetes represents an intermediate glycemic state that may overlap with both neighboring groups, we additionally evaluated two binary tasks.
For the normal-versus-impaired task, participants with prediabetes or diabetes were combined into an impaired-glycemia group.
For the normal-versus-diabetes task, participants with prediabetes were excluded.

The binary tasks used the same model architectures and nested cross-validation framework as the three-class task, with the output layers modified for two-class prediction and class-weighted loss calculated using two classes.
Results for the binary tasks are reported at the participant level in Table 3.

text.text: A secondary analysis predicting continuous HbA1c levels is described in Supplementary Materials Section D.
All models were trained and evaluated using nested five-fold cross-validation.
Participants were assigned to five stratified outer folds, with both eyes from a given participant retained in the same fold to prevent information leakage.
In each iteration, four outer folds were used for model development and the remaining fold was held out for evaluation.
Hyperparameter selection was conducted exclusively within the outer training set using an inner stratified five-fold crossvalidation procedure.
The selected model was then evaluated on the held-out outer test fold.
This process was repeated until each outer fold had served once as the test set.
Performance metrics were calculated separately for each outer test fold and summarized as the mean ± standard deviation across the five folds.
Performance evaluation.

For the three-class task, accuracy, F1 score, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and positive predictive value (PPV) were calculated for each class and then macro-averaged across the three classes.
For binary tasks, the corresponding binary classification metrics were reported.
Confusion matrices were constructed by pooling predictions from the five held-out outer test folds.
To interpret model predictions, we applied Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) 19 to the CNN model as it was the best performing model.

text.text: Grad-CAM generates saliency maps by highlighting regions in the input image that contribute most strongly to the model's predictions.
For each participant, Grad-CAM was computed from the final convolutional layer of the CNN on participants in the outer fold held out for evaluation.

To obtain a robust representation of model attention rather than individual sample variability, we averaged the per-eye Grad-CAMs across all test eyes, stratified by confusion-matrix cell (true × predicted class), to visualize attention patterns in both correctly classified and misclassified cases (Figure 6).

This study shows that CMM-based FLIO mean lifetime maps carry a measurable signal related to glycemic status.
Group-averaged τCMM lifetime differed significantly across glycemic groups in the SSC, and the difference persisted after age adjustment.
All three FLIO models outperformed an age-only classifier, suggesting that the FLIO signal is not simply a proxy for age, although individual-level discrimination of glycemic status remained modest.

By computing τCMM maps, we reduced complex spatiotemporal photon-counting data to interpretable two-dimensional representations, enabling the application of standard image-based deep learning models for glycemic classification.
The τCMM values reported in this study should not be interpreted as equivalent to conventional FLIO 𝜏 𝑚 values derived from multi-exponential fitting.

First, τCMM was computed without instrument response function (IRF) deconvolution: the timing-offset correction removes the electronic delay but not the effect of the finite duration of the excitation pulse, 20 and even after background and timing-offset correction, central-window values (approximately 4.7-5.0 ns in the SSC and 3.6-3.8 ns in the LSC) remain much longer than fitted 𝜏 𝑚 values reported in the FLIO literature.

Visualization of aggregated τCMM maps revealed longer τCMM in prediabetic and, more markedly, diabetic participants across most of the macula, with the largest differences at the fovea (Figures 2 and 3).

text.text: These differences may reflect metabolic alterations in retinal fluorophores associated with chronic hyperglycemia; they persisted after age adjustment and after excluding participants with self-reported diabetic retinopathy.
That the models outperformed an age-only classifier suggests that FLIO captures diabetes-related retinal signals beyond those attributable to age.

Discrimination in our study (best AUROC 0.67, CNN, normal versus diabetes) was also lower than that reported by Schmidt et al. for classifying nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy versus healthy controls (AUROC 0.865), 6 likely because only 8.9% of our diabetic participants reported DR, so that our diabetes group largely represents an earlier disease stage, and because our estimates were obtained from patients in the evaluation folds rather than from a logistic-regression model fitted to a small case-control sample (33 cases and 28 controls).

text.text: This phenomenon suggests that while FLIO captures metabolic differences between glycemic states, the signal may be insufficient to recover fine-grained variation in HbA1c.
HbA1c reflects systemic glycemic exposure rather than localized retinal metabolism, which may limit the predictive capacity of retinal imaging alone.
Overall, these results suggest that while τCMM maps contain information related to glycemic states, the separation between classes is subtle, leading to overlapping predictions across categories.
The consistent performance across different model types further indicates that the limitation may stem from the intrinsic signal in the data rather than model capacity.
These findings have important implications for the use of FLIO in clinical applications.
While FLIO may serve as a promising noninvasive screening tool for identifying metabolic abnormalities, it is unlikely to replace blood-based HbA1c measurements for precise glycemic quantification.
Several limitations should be noted.
First, this study used a single dataset, and external validation is needed to assess generalizability.
Second, only FLIO-derived inputs were included; integrating FLIO with other imaging modalities such as OCT or fundus photography may further improve predictive performance.
Third, outcome labels combined self-reported diagnosis and treatment and a single HbA1c measurement; diabetes duration was not available, and self-reported information may be imprecise.

Fourth, diabetic macular edema status, panretinal or focal laser history, and lens status (phakic vs. pseudophakic) are not recorded in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) and could not be assessed; comorbidity information was limited to self-report.

Fifth, no measured instrument response function is available for these acquisitions, precluding reliable multi-exponential reconvolution fitting; comparison of τCMM against fitted 𝜏 𝑚 on datasets with measured IRFs remains future work.

In summary, FLIO-derived τCMM maps contain spatial information related to diabetes status beyond age alone, but the signal is too weak to support accurate classification of glycemic states at the individual level.
These findings delineate both the potential and the challenges of FLIO-based metabolic assessment.

text.text: The mean lifetimes were converted from bin units to physical time using the frame time recorded in the FLIO metadata which specifies the temporal spacing between bins.
The mean fluorescence lifetime at each pixel was computed as: where Δ𝑡 denotes the frame time per bin.
This process yielded a two-dimensional spatial map of the mean fluorescence lifetime for each eye and spectral channel.
The main difference between this uncorrected method and the corrected method presented in the main text is the lack of background-and time-offset-corrections.
We assessed the impact of the intensity filtering, which excludes pixels with fewer than 50 photons, in estimation of the τCMM mean lifetime maps.
For the corrected τCMM mean lifetime maps, the median proportion of retained pixels was 99.84% for SSC (IQR, 99.44%-99.99%) and 100% for LSC (IQR, 99.87%-100%).
Pixels were excluded in 142 SSC eyes (4.1%) and 84 LSC eyes (2.4%).
Excluded pixels were predominantly located at frame borders and in dim regions of a small number of low-quality scans.

Therefore, the intensity threshold is unlikely to have systematically removed pixels from low-intensity anatomical structures or materially altered the spatial distribution of retinal lifetime signals.

To assess whether FLIO-derived features can capture continuous glycemic variation, we trained models to predict HbA1c values directly from τCMM maps.

The same model architectures described for classification (CNN, ResNet18, and XGBoost) were used, with the primary modification being the replacement of the final classification layer with a regression output layer.
Models were trained using the same procedures as in the classification setting.
For deep learning models, Smooth L1 loss was used for optimization, while XGBoost models were trained using regression objectives.
Model performance was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE).
Agreement between predicted and observed HbA1c values was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis.
Regression models trained to predict continuous HbA1c values achieved a test mean absolute error of approximately 0.76.
However, predicted values showed strong collapse toward the mean HbA1c level, indicating that the model failed to capture meaningful variation in HbA1c across patients.

The XGBoost hist tree method was used throughout.
Hyperparameter names follow the XGBoost Python API conventions.
The deep models were trained with class-weighted cross-entropy.
Weights followed the standard scikitlearn formulation, where N is the total number of training participants in the fold, K is the number of classes, and nᵢ is the count of class i in that fold.
Weights were renormalized to unit mean before use.
The same formulation was applied to the binary tasks with K = 2.
A global seed of 42 was used for the outer cross-validation.
The inner cross-validation seeds were offset by the outer-fold index (seed = 42 + k for outer fold k) so that inner splits did not overlap across folds.
Per-eye encoder outputs (256-dimensional for CNN, 512-dimensional for ResNet-18) were aggregated to per-participant representations by mean pooling over each participant's available eyes (1 or 2).
For the participants with a single eye, the singleton embedding was used directly without zero-padding.
Participant predictions were obtained from the classifier head applied to the pooled embedding.
Right-eye maps were mirrored horizontally to the left-eye orientation before encoding (laterality canonicalization).
In the FLIO + age models, age scaled as (age -60)/10 was concatenated to the pooled embedding before the classifier head.
Then, we removed ambient background counts.

For each pixel, we estimated the background rate 𝑏(𝑥, 𝑦) (counts per time bin) as the mean count over the time bins preceding the fluorescence rise, averaged over a 15 × 15-pixel neighborhood to suppress photon noise.

The background was subtracted from every time bin of the active acquisition window, 𝑡 𝑠 ≤ 𝑡 ≤ 𝑡 𝑒 , giving the net photon count for each pixel location (𝑥, 𝑦): 𝑁 net (𝑥, 𝑦) = ∑[𝐼(𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑡) -𝑏(𝑥, 𝑦)] 𝑡 𝑒 𝑡=𝑡 𝑠 , where 𝐼(𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑡) represents the photon count at pixel (𝑥, 𝑦) in time bin 𝑡.
Pixels with insufficient photon counts produce unstable lifetime estimates.
Therefore, pixels with net photon counts lower than 50 were excluded from analysis.
